content:
During the holiday, I spent a night at Muyunshe, a hot-spring retreat opened by a friend in Qijia Town, Longhua County.
Compared with the livelier hot-spring resorts along the roadside in Qijia, I actually prefer this place.
The property covers several thousand square meters, with gardens, vegetable plots, tents, hot springs, barbecue areas, and even a basketball court. Everything is spread out naturally, with plenty of space to slow down.
I stayed for one night and headed home the next day.
On the way back, I passed Kuanguang Supermarket’s Lishui store and stopped to wash the car.
That was when I noticed that the benefits for Gold Members had been upgraded again: the member car-wash area now has a second bay.
That means much less waiting.
While waiting, my family and I did a quick calculation.
The Gold Membership costs 188 yuan a year, with 30 yuan returned, so the effective cost is 158 yuan.
Members can use the car wash once a week. Spread over 52 weeks, that works out to only about 3 yuan per wash.
And this is not just a quick rinse.
The whole process takes a little over ten minutes and includes two rounds of foam, high-pressure rinsing, liquid wax, and air drying.
Once you factor in the equipment, water, electricity, consumables, and maintenance, three yuan clearly does not cover the cost.
If this were a dedicated car-wash business, the economics would make no sense.
A professional car wash needs to make money from washing cars, ideally with additional services such as waxing, polishing, or interior cleaning.
The core service itself has to be profitable.
A supermarket works differently.
Car washing is not Kuanguang’s main business.
The once-a-week design is easy to understand: it gives members a reason to come back to the Lishui flagship store every week.
The car gets washed, and the customer is already there.
Once you are at the supermarket, there is a good chance you will go inside and pick up fruit, vegetables, milk, household goods, or something else you need anyway.
For a retailer whose core business is fast-moving consumer goods, whether the car wash itself makes money may not be the most important question.
Its real value is that it adds convenience around the core business and creates another reason for customers to return.
So some services that look obviously “unprofitable” can make perfect sense once you look at the entire retail model instead of judging them in isolation.
It also made me think about a familiar consumer reaction.
A lot of people see the words “annual membership fee” and immediately think:
I have to pay just to join? No thanks.
But the picture can look very different when you calculate the value another way.
A typical car wash might charge 300 yuan for ten washes and throw in two more, which works out to around 25 yuan per visit.
By contrast, if you already shop regularly at Kuanguang’s Lishui store, the car-wash benefit alone brings the effective cost of each wash down to about 3 yuan.
That is roughly one-tenth of the price of a regular car wash.
Three yuan does not even take you very far on a shared bike these days.
Of course, the benefit only matters if you actually use it.
The worst kind of membership is one that makes people spend money simply because they want to “get their money’s worth.”
But if you already need groceries, already visit the supermarket, and already wash your car, then benefits like these are worth paying attention to.
Working inside a retail company, I have seen this logic firsthand.
Many of these services are not designed to generate profit on their own.
Parking, car washing, member events, loyalty points, rest areas, and other add-on services all follow a similar idea:
Make the customer’s visit easier, more comfortable, and more worthwhile—and give them a reason to come back more often.
The retailer gains traffic and goodwill.
The customer gets genuine convenience.
If both sides benefit, why not?
This is one membership perk that is genuinely worth using.
After washing the car, I parked it in my underground garage at home.
Since I did not expect to drive for a few days, I pulled out a disposable transparent car cover and put it over the freshly washed car.
Within moments, something looked wrong.
The engine was still hot from the drive, and the body still held some moisture from the wash.
The transparent cover quickly began to puff up.
It looked like I had wrapped the whole car inside a giant clear balloon.
I watched it for a few seconds, then removed it immediately.
Apparently, even “protection” can be a bad idea if you rush it.
Haha.
summary: An annual membership costs 188 yuan, with 30 yuan returned. Use the weekly car wash regularly and it works out to roughly 3 yuan per visit. What looks like a loss on paper can make perfect sense in retail.
title: A Three-Yuan Car Wash—and Why the Math Actually Works

content:
During this National Day holiday, I found myself tinkering with ZISAI again.
I had only meant to fix a few things that had been bothering me. Once I started, though, it was hard to stop.
The homepage, hero image, logo, navigation, Hugo, PaperMod, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare, DNS, CNAME records, 301 redirects… I worked through them all, right down to a small problem with sharing pages on WeChat.
Looking over the site again this morning, I finally felt that this round of work could pause. Most of the problems I could currently identify had been addressed.
A small problem worth following through The most memorable issue turned out to be sharing a webpage as a WeChat card.
The page opened normally. Sending its URL directly worked too. But sharing it from a browser to a WeChat contact produced a red exclamation mark. Stranger still, posting it to Moments first and forwarding it from there worked.
I tried Safari, Chrome and Edge. Eventually, the trail led to the sharing image. The file was too large. After I compressed it, sharing worked again.
These days, I have gradually settled on a habit: use WebP for web images where suitable, with a quality setting around 82, while checking that they still look right. Q82 is no magic number. It is simply a balance that currently feels comfortable to me: smaller files, with little visible loss.
I may forget the number one day. I am less likely to forget the process of tracking down the problem.
Technical details are often like that. The answer may fade; the way you found it stays.
Work is a responsibility; ZISAI is self-directed I spent much of the holiday sitting at my computer. From the outside, it probably looked much like being at work. It felt quite different.
Work brings goals, deadlines and collaboration. A sense of responsibility drives me to deliver.
With ZISAI, nobody tells me what the site should look like or when it needs to be finished. If the hero image feels wrong, I change it. If the logo is almost right, I adjust it again. If I do not understand a problem, I try a few more things.
Whether to do it, when to do it and how far to take it are my decisions. I enjoy that freedom. I often feel more creative with fewer constraints. There are still standards and expectations; they come from me.
Making something of my own As the work went on, it began to feel less like routine website maintenance and more like making a piece of work I could call my own.
Should an image be a little softer? How large should the logo be? Is there enough space on the page? How can Chengde’s character appear naturally? Does the button feel right in that position? Is a few dozen extra kilobytes worth it?
Each decision is small. Together, they create a sense of coherence.
It reminds me a little of woodworking, or editing photographs. Other people may not notice exactly what changed. I know, though, and I keep thinking it could be a little better.
At that point, technology becomes part of the work itself: code, images, structure, speed and detail all belong to the same whole.
Twenty-eight years later I started ZISAI in 1998, when the internet itself felt new. Forums, chat rooms, webpages and servers—everything invited exploration.
Twenty-eight years later, the technology has changed completely. Now I tinker with Hugo, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare, WebP, Open Graph images and countless frontend details. The website is very different from the one I began with.
Yet something seems unchanged. When I see a problem, I still want to understand it. When something could be better, I still want to improve it.
Perhaps what has lasted is the habit of trying to make things a little more complete.
Time passes. That impulse remains. There is no assignment and no deadline. I simply want the site to come a little closer to the version I have in mind.
A stopping point, for now This morning, I looked through the site once more. Most of the issues I could think of had been handled.
Of course, a website is never truly finished. I will keep writing and making changes. But this stage can come to a pause.
Being able to immerse yourself in something is an ability. Staying interested in it for twenty-eight years says something about you, too. I have kept going with exercise, English, Japanese and information technology in much the same spirit.
Knowing when to stop is probably another ability worth keeping.
So this round of rebuilding ZISAI during the 2026 National Day holiday ends here, for now.
This afternoon, I am going to the hot springs.
The computer is closed.
As for the next problem—I’ll wait until it turns up.
summary: During the National Day holiday, I rebuilt ZISAI once again. Work carries responsibility; this website runs on personal curiosity. Technology, design and small details became part of something I wanted to make well.
title: ZISAI at 28: Technology Changes, Habits Stay

content:
I am Shen Nan (沈楠), a technology practitioner whose career has taken me from radio communications to the internet, cloud computing and artificial intelligence.
I serve as Director, Vice President and CIO of Chengde Kuangguang Holdings Group and hold a master’s degree in informatics from J. F. Oberlin University in Japan. After years working in communications networks, internet services, data centers and software development, I moved into retail, where I oversee enterprise information systems, digitalization and technology architecture.
In 1998, I began building ZISAI (zisai.com), an early website within Chengde’s postal and telecommunications community.
From single-sideband radio, point-to-point data links, dial-up networks and the early web to broadband, data centers, online games, enterprise systems, hyperconverged infrastructure, IoT, cloud-native systems and AI, the technologies have kept changing. What I try to do has remained much the same:
Understand a problem, break it down, and solve it with technology that is as simple and reliable as possible.
I still maintain ZISAI today. It is a place for technology, Chengde, everyday life, memories of the city and small things worth keeping.
From communications to the internet My work with technology began in the 1990s.
In 1993, I joined a military communications unit, working with radio, single-sideband (SSB) and double-sideband (DSB) communications, computers and data transmission. Before internet access became widespread, connecting people and computers often meant radios, serial ports, modems and point-to-point links.
Around 1995, I began writing point-to-point communications programs in C and exploring BBSs, dial-up networks and early online communities. After 1997, I turned to the web, online information services and early internet applications.
In 1998, I joined a telecommunications operator and started the website that became ZISAI. The internet has been a continuing thread through my work and life ever since.
ZISAI and Chengde’s early internet ZISAI began in 1998 as a very small website.
As broadband spread, it grew to include a portal, forums, chat rooms, blogs, a flea market, software downloads and audio and video services. For many of Chengde’s early internet users, it became part of a shared memory.
Around 2001, I was developing and maintaining these services with PHP, MySQL, C++, ASP and Pascal. They included the ZISAI forum, online chat rooms and blogs, a flea market, FreeICQ local instant messaging, the MUD Xia Ke Xing, and local broadband media services.
In 2002, I developed Rehe Fengyun (热河风云), a multiplayer online game with a local cultural setting.
These projects may look simple today, but they document a local internet’s transition from dial-up to broadband. They were also my first sustained experience of building and operating internet services from end to end.
Telecommunications, broadband and data centers From 1998 to 2014, my work at a telecommunications operator expanded from computers and data communications to broadband networks, business systems, internet data centers (IDC) and internet operations.
I worked on or took responsibility for ADSL business systems, network operations systems, broadband streaming services, data center services and internet content partnerships.
Between roughly 2003 and 2006, I helped introduce and operate local server groups for games including 科洛斯, 坦克宝贝, NetEase’s 梦幻西游 and 大话西游. All of the server groups were named “避暑山庄”, after Chengde’s Mountain Resort.
As online game account security became a growing concern, I also designed and developed a dynamic-password authentication system to improve account protection.
Around 2009, my work increasingly involved IDC, ICT and internet infrastructure. I helped bring relevant business activities of companies including Tencent, Youku and Alibaba to Chengde. This experience gave me a more systematic understanding of networks, systems, data centers and high-availability architecture.
From telecommunications to retail digitalization In 2014, I left the telecommunications operator and joined Chengde Kuangguang Holdings Group as Vice President and CIO.
The business environment changed, but the questions were familiar. How could systems become more stable? How could data create practical value? How could online and offline operations connect? How could fragmented systems work together? How should security, performance, cost and business efficiency be balanced?
For more than a decade, my work has centered on enterprise information systems, retail digitalization, infrastructure, data, security and software development. It has included e-commerce, stored-value cards, business intelligence, hyperconverged infrastructure, cloud platforms, IoT, cybersecurity, disaster recovery, the WeChat ecosystem and AI.
Selected technology projects Year Project Work and technologies 1998– ZISAI Portal, forums, chat rooms, blogs and a flea market; now maintained as a personal website. Web, PHP, MySQL, Hugo. 2001 ADSL service order system Independently developed a system for receiving and routing broadband service requests. ASP, SQL Server. 2002 Rehe Fengyun Developed and operated a local multiplayer game rooted in Chengde’s culture. Pascal, network programming. 2003 Chengde broadband streaming platform Video-on-demand and streaming services for broadband users. RealServer, Linux, PHP. 2003–2006 Local online game server groups Helped build and operate Chengde server groups for several online games. Linux, IDC, network operations. 2006 Dynamic-password authentication Designed authentication mechanisms for online game accounts. C++, security authentication. 2016 Hyperconverged and hybrid cloud infrastructure Consolidated servers, compute, storage and virtualization into a group-wide platform. VMware, Docker, Kubernetes. 2016–2021 Omnichannel electronic stored-value cards Card management, electronic redemption and transaction security, including dynamic QR-code encryption in Go. 2020 ESRS health check-in system Independently developed a commercial-site health check-in and data management system during the pandemic. C++, MySQL. 2023 Group-wide IoT platform Connectivity and monitoring for cold chains, energy, environments, equipment and security. Python, MQTT. 2024 Core data disaster recovery Cross-system and cross-device backup and recovery for core business data. High availability and disaster recovery architecture. 2025 Kuangguang digital management platform An integrated platform for retail operations, data and management; selected as an annual outstanding retail digitalization practice by the China Commerce Association for General Merchandise. Data platforms, distributed architecture, AI. 2025 AI staff assessment system Explored using large language models to assist with assessment data analysis, evaluation writing and feedback. A technology journey spanning more than thirty years 1993–1997: Radio and computers. From SSB and DSB radio to computers and data communications. 1998–2001: The internet and the web. Joined a telecommunications operator, began ZISAI, and worked with Perl, ASP, PHP, MySQL and C++. 2002–2008: Broadband, communities and online games. Developed Rehe Fengyun, built chat rooms, forums and streaming services, and worked on game servers and security authentication. 2009–2014: Data centers and telecommunications operations. Led work in IDC, ICT, data communications, internet business development and mobile network business management. 2014–2020: Enterprise systems and cloud architecture. Built retail e-commerce, card systems, BI, virtualization, hyperconverged infrastructure and enterprise cloud systems. 2021–2024: IoT, data and security. Continued practical work with Go, IoT, enterprise and payment security, WeChat and core data disaster recovery. 2025 onward: AI and retail digitalization. Began applying large language models, data analysis and AI to real business situations. The names of the technologies keep changing. My curiosity and interest in using them to solve practical problems have stayed with me.
Education I studied at J. F. Oberlin University Graduate School in Japan and earned a master’s degree in informatics in 2021.
Studying abroad let me revisit more than twenty years of practical work through research and academic inquiry. It also strengthened my preference for starting with small, concrete questions that can be observed and tested. That approach shapes how I write on ZISAI today.
Professional and community roles Current roles Director, Vice President and CIO, Chengde Kuangguang Holdings Group Supervisor, Chengde Kuangguang Supermarket Group Member, Digital Technology Application Committee of the China Chain Store & Franchise Association Member, Digitalization Committee of the China Commerce Association for General Merchandise Vice Chair and Executive Chair, Chengde Internet Association Chair, Chengde Federation of Internet Industry Trade Unions Council Member, Chengde Police Association President, Shuangqiao District E-commerce Association, Chengde Earlier experience Department Section Chief, China Unicom’s Chengde branch Secretary of the Communist Youth League Committee, China Unicom’s Chengde branch Service in a military communications unit, 1993–1997 Recognition and industry experience Recognition over the years has included National Outstanding CIO; the Digital Technology Innovation Award at the China International Digital Economy Expo; communications-industry QC group activity assessor qualification from the China Association of Communications Enterprises; Hebei “Knowledge-based Employee”; the Chengde “Shen Nan Innovation Studio”; and Chengde honors for young skilled professionals, science and technology work, commerce expertise and science communication.
These are part of the record. But I am more inclined to remember the systems built, the code written and the feeling when a problem was finally solved.
About ZISAI Founded in 1998, ZISAI has passed through the eras of portals, forums, chat rooms and blogs, and from desktop and broadband internet to mobile internet and AI.
Today, zisai.com is my personal digital space. I write about:
Technology: software, networks, servers, Hugo, Go, AI and practical work. Retail: digitalization and business observations grounded in specific problems. Chengde: the Mountain Resort, Rehe, the old city, internet history and local memories. Life: travel, cars, exercise and questions that arise in ordinary days. The past: gathering personal and urban memories before they fade. Not everything worth recording has to be a major event. Much of what makes up a life consists of small things that seemed ordinary at the time.
Places hold stories. Everyday life shines.
Technology and life I still enjoy writing code and exploring new tools. My interests include Go, Python, SQL, Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, Hugo, cloud computing, virtualization, network and information security, IoT, data analysis, large language models and AI.
My approach is simple:
Use the simplest possible logic to solve complex problems.
Away from technology, I enjoy walking, driving trips, music, keeping fish, growing orchids and quietly tinkering with my website.
I started ZISAI in 1998. Today, I can still spend hours adjusting a page, an image or a few lines of code. Technologies and tools change. Curiosity and the habit of keeping a record may well remain.

Profile last updated in October 2026. English editorial version based on the Chinese profile; organization names and titles are descriptive translations.
summary:
I am Shen Nan (沈楠), a technology practitioner whose career has taken me from radio communications to the internet, cloud computing and artificial intelligence.

I serve as Director, Vice President and CIO of Chengde Kuangguang Holdings Group and hold a master’s degree in informatics from J. F. Oberlin University in Japan. After years working in communications networks, internet services, data centers and software development, I moved into retail, where I oversee enterprise information systems, digitalization and technology architecture.
title: About Shen Nan
